vignette: A 52-year-old man presents with progressive weakness of the right upper extremity. Neurologic examination demonstrates marked spasticity with a pronator catch, hyperactive biceps and triceps reflexes, a positive Hoffmann sign, and an extensor plantar response on the right. Fasciculations and muscle atrophy are absent.
question: Which motor system localization is indicated by these clinical findings?
options: Lower motor neuron lesion of the anterior horn cells
Peripheral neuropathy of the radial nerve
Upper motor neuron lesion rostral to C5
Neuromuscular junction transmission defect
Primary myopathic process

explanation.why_correct: The constellation of spasticity, hyperreflexia, pathological reflexes (Hoffmann sign, extensor plantar response/Babinski), and absence of fasciculations/atrophy represents the hallmark of an Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) lesion. Because the right upper extremity reflexes and tone are increased, the lesion must lie rostral to the C5 cervical motor segments (e.g., motor cortex, internal capsule, brainstem, or high cervical cord).
distractors: Lower motor neuron lesions produce flaccidity, hyporeflexia, muscle atrophy, and visible fasciculations, not spasticity.
Radial neuropathy produces wrist and finger drop with diminished brachioradialis/triceps reflexes without spasticity or extensor plantar responses.
Neuromuscular junction defects produce fatigable weakness without tone changes or pathological reflexes.
Myopathies cause symmetric proximal weakness with normal or diminished reflexes and no pyramidal signs.
explanation.key_point: Upper motor neuron lesions are characterized by spasticity, hyperreflexia, and pathological reflexes (Babinski, Hoffmann) without denervation atrophy.

vignette: A 64-year-old woman presents with acute-onset right facial droop, slurred speech, and right arm weakness. Sensory examination reveals intact primary modalities (light touch, pinprick, vibration), but the patient cannot identify a key placed in her right hand with eyes closed (astereognosis) and fails to identify numbers drawn on her right palm (agraphästhesia). Language testing reveals fluent paraphasic speech with impaired comprehension.
question: Which neuroanatomic level accounts for cortical sensory loss coupled with language dysfunction?
options: Left thalamic sensory nuclei (VPL/VPM)
Left cerebral cortex (perisylvian and anterior parietal cortex)
Left posterior limb of the internal capsule
Left basis pontis
Cervical posterior columns

explanation.why_correct: Cortical sensory loss (astereognosis, agraphesthesia, two-point discrimination deficit) with intact primary sensory modalities indicates dysfunction of the contralateral somatosensory cortex (parietal lobe). Concomitant fluent aphasia with comprehension impairment localizes definitively to the left hemisphere cerebral cortex, as subcortical or brainstem lesions do not produce cortical sensory signs or fluent aphasia.
distractors: Thalamic lesions impair primary sensory modalities (pinprick, temperature, vibration) rather than isolated discriminative cortical modalities, and do not cause fluent aphasia.
Internal capsule lesions produce dense pure motor or sensorimotor hemiparesis without cortical deficits such as aphasia or astereognosis.
Basis pontis lesions produce crossed cranial nerve deficits or pure motor hemiparesis, sparing language and parietal sensations.
Posterior column spinal cord lesions impair vibration and joint position sense bilaterally or ipsilaterally, without speech or language disturbance.
explanation.key_point: Astereognosis and agraphesthesia in the presence of intact primary sensation localize specifically to the contralateral cerebral cortex.

source_quote: Alternating hemiplegia results in “crossed” signs, with CN involvement ipsilateral to the lesion, and contralateral hemiparesis or hemiplegia.
vignette: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden double vision and left-sided body weakness. Neurologic examination shows a complete right third cranial nerve palsy with ptosis and a dilated, unreactive pupil, accompanied by left-sided spastic hemiparesis affecting the face, arm, and leg.
question: What classic localization principle is demonstrated by this patient's clinical presentation?
options: Cerebral hemispheric cortical stroke with uncal herniation
Alternating (crossed) brainstem syndrome localizing the lesion to the ipsilateral midbrain
Cervical spinal cord hemicord lesion (Brown-Séquard syndrome)
Polyradiculopathy affecting cranial nerves and spinal roots
Bilateral internal capsule lacunar infarcts

explanation.why_correct: This is the classic prototype of an 'alternating' or 'crossed' brainstem syndrome (Weber syndrome). The cranial nerve deficit (CN III) is ipsilateral to the lesion and marks the rostral-caudal level (midbrain), while the long tract sign (corticospinal hemiplegia) is contralateral because the corticospinal tract decussates lower in the medulla.
distractors: Cortical strokes do not produce lower motor neuron third cranial nerve palsies; uncal herniation causes depressed consciousness and is preceded by severe intracranial mass effect.
Spinal cord hemicord lesions do not cause cranial nerve III palsy or facial weakness.
Polyradiculopathy causes flaccid areflexic weakness, not spastic pyramidal hemiparesis.
Capsular lacunar strokes produce pure motor hemiparesis without nuclear or fascicular ocular motor cranial nerve palsies.
explanation.key_point: Ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy combined with contralateral long-tract motor or sensory signs is the cardinal hallmark of brainstem localization.

vignette: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for acute left leg weakness following an emotional dispute. On examination in the supine position, the examiner places a hand under the patient's right heel while asking her to flex the left hip against resistance. Normal involuntary downward pressure is felt under the examiner's right hand. Pinprick sensory testing reveals an abrupt, sharp loss of sensation beginning precisely at the abdominal midline.
question: Which diagnostic sign and localization interpretation is most accurate?
options: Brown-Séquard hemicord syndrome with accurate dermatomal sensory cut-off
Anterior cerebral artery territory infarction with unilateral leg weakness
Positive Hoover sign with midline sensory splitting, indicating non-organic (functional) weakness
Conus medullaris compression with asymmetric radiculopathy
Femoral nerve compression neuropathy

explanation.why_correct: The Hoover sign evaluates involuntary extension of the contralateral hip during voluntary hip flexion of the paretic leg. Normal downward pressure in the opposite heel indicates intact subcortical motor pathways. Midline splitting of sensation precisely at the anatomical sagittal line is non-anatomical because sensory nerve fibers overlap by 1 to 2 cm across the midline.
distractors: Brown-Séquard syndrome produces contralateral pain/temperature loss starting 1-2 segments below the lesion with preserved ipsilateral pain/temp, never exact midline splitting.
ACA infarction causes true upper motor neuron leg weakness with hyperreflexia and Babinski sign, with negative Hoover sign.
Conus medullaris lesions produce symmetric saddle anesthesia, sphincter dysfunction, and mixed UMN/LMN signs.
Femoral neuropathy causes weakness limited to quadriceps with absent knee jerk and sensory loss over anterior thigh/medial calf.
explanation.key_point: Hoover sign and exact cutaneous midline sensory splitting are reliable clinical indicators of non-organic (functional) neurological deficits.

source_quote: weakness or paralysis of involved muscles, flaccidity, hypotonia, decreased or absent muscle stretch reflexes (hyporeflexia or areflexia), and eventually muscle atrophy
vignette: A 45-year-old construction worker presents with progressive weakness in his right arm. Examination reveals profound muscle atrophy in the biceps and brachioradialis, prominent fasciculations, absent biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, but normal sensation and no spasticity.
question: Which combination of findings defines this clinical presentation?
options: Upper motor neuron lesion characterized by spasticity, hyperreflexia, and clonus
Lower motor neuron lesion characterized by flaccidity, fasciculations, and hyporeflexia
Neuromuscular junction disorder with fatigable ptosis and normal bulk
Primary myopathy with symmetrical proximal weakness and preserved reflexes

explanation.why_correct: Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions disrupt alpha motor neurons in the anterior horn or peripheral nerve, causing flaccid weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, and loss of tendon jerks.
distractors: Upper motor neuron lesions produce spastic hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses (Babinski sign).
Neuromuscular junction disorders produce fatigable weakness without fasciculations or early atrophy.
Myopathies present with symmetric proximal limb weakness with preserved deep tendon reflexes until late stages.
explanation.key_point: Muscle atrophy, visible fasciculations, and absent tendon jerks are pathognomonic hallmarks of a lower motor neuron lesion.

vignette: A 58-year-old woman is evaluated for leg weakness. Tapping the right patellar tendon elicits a brisk quadriceps contraction followed by three beats of clonus, while plantar stimulation produces great toe extension and fanning of other toes.
question: Where is the lesion definitively localized relative to the lumbar motor neurons?
options: Above the L2–L4 spinal segments interrupting the descending corticospinal tract
At the L3–L4 anterior horn cells causing localized anterior motor neuron injury
Within the femoral nerve trunk causing mixed sensory-motor denervation
In the posterior columns sparing the descending motor pathways

explanation.why_correct: Hyperreflexia, clonus, and a positive Babinski sign are classic upper motor neuron (UMN) signs indicating disruption of descending corticospinal fibers rostral to the segmental reflex arc (L2–L4).
distractors: Anterior horn cell lesions produce lower motor neuron signs (hyporeflexia, flaccidity), not hyperreflexia or Babinski.
Femoral nerve lesions diminish the patellar reflex (areflexia) and never cause extensor plantar responses.
Posterior column lesions cause sensory ataxia and loss of vibration/proprioception, leaving plantar responses flexor.
explanation.key_point: A positive Babinski sign combined with patellar hyperreflexia and clonus confirms a corticospinal (UMN) tract lesion above the L2–L4 spinal level.

vignette: A 34-year-old woman notes that while showering, hot water feels cool on her left leg and trunk up to the level of the umbilicus (T10). Pinprick sensation is severely impaired in the same distribution, but vibration and joint position sense remain completely intact bilaterally.
question: Which tract is selectively damaged and where does it decussate?
options: Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis), which decussate in the medulla as internal arcuate fibers
Corticospinal tract, which decussates at the cervicomedullary junction into the lateral column
Spinocerebellar tract, which enters the cerebellum via the restiform body without thalamic projection
Spinothalamic tract, which decussates 1 to 2 segments above its spinal entry level in the anterior white commissure

explanation.why_correct: The spinothalamic tract transmits pain and temperature; its second-order axons cross in the anterior white commissure 1–2 segments rostral to entry. A contralateral loss of pain/temperature indicates damage to this anterolateral tract.
distractors: The dorsal columns transmit vibration and joint position sense and ascend uncrossed in the cord until the medullary nuclei.
The lateral corticospinal tract is a descending motor pathway and does not mediate cutaneous thermoanalgesia.
The spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum and do not cause conscious sensory loss.
explanation.key_point: Dissociated sensory loss (loss of pain/temperature with preserved vibration/proprioception) reflects selective anterolateral spinothalamic tract impairment.

vignette: A 67-year-old man has acute right hemiparesis and right hemianesthesia. Neurologic exam reveals right homonymous hemianopia, expressive nonfluent aphasia, and impaired gaze preference to the left, but no limb ataxia.
question: Which feature most reliably confirms a cerebral cortical localization rather than an internal capsule lacunar infarct?
options: Dense pure motor hemiparesis equally affecting face, arm, and leg
Preservation of pupillary light reflexes and extraocular range on doll's head maneuver
Hyperreflexia in the paretic limbs with extensor plantar response
Presence of aphasia and conjugate gaze preference toward the lesion

explanation.why_correct: Higher cortical cognitive deficits (aphasia, apraxia, agnosia, neglect) and cortical gaze deviation toward the damaged hemisphere localize the lesion to the cerebral cortex, ruling out deep pure subcortical capsular lacunes.
distractors: Dense hemiparesis equally affecting face, arm, and leg (pure motor stroke) is the classic hallmark of internal capsule lacunar infarction.
Preserved pupillary reflexes and positive oculocephalic reflexes merely exclude midbrain or pontine brainstem lesions.
Hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses occur in both cortical and subcortical upper motor neuron injuries.
explanation.key_point: Cortical 'neighborhood signs' such as aphasia, neglect, and apraxia definitively distinguish hemispheric cortical strokes from deep subcortical lacunar syndromes.

source_quote: ipsilateral loss of proprioceptive function below the level of the lesion due to interruption of ascending fibers in the posterior column
vignette: A 29-year-old man is stabbed in the mid-back. Examination shows spastic weakness of the right leg with brisk reflexes below the injury, and loss of vibration and joint position sense in the right leg. Pinprick and temperature sensation are lost in the left leg and left trunk, beginning a few segments below the level of injury.
question: Which lesion best explains these findings?
options: Left half of the thoracic spinal cord
Center of the thoracic spinal cord (central cord lesion)
Right half of the thoracic spinal cord
Left cerebral peduncle
Both dorsal columns of the thoracic spinal cord

explanation.why_correct: Damage to the right half of the cord interrupts the right corticospinal tract (ipsilateral spastic paralysis below the lesion) and the right posterior column (ipsilateral loss of position and vibration sense). Pain and temperature fibers decussate in the anterior commissure and ascend in the contralateral spinothalamic tract, so their loss appears on the opposite (left) side.
distractors: A left hemicord lesion would put the spastic weakness and the loss of position and vibration sense on the left, and the pain and temperature loss on the right.

A central cord lesion produces a segmental, dissociated sensory loss (pain and temperature affected, position sense preserved) and does not cause unilateral spastic weakness with ipsilateral posterior column loss.
A cerebral peduncle lesion would cause a contralateral hemiparesis including the face and typically cranial nerve involvement, not a leg-only pattern with a crossed sensory level.
Bilateral dorsal column lesions would impair vibration and position sense on both sides but would not cause spastic weakness or loss of pain and temperature sensation.
explanation.key_point: A hemicord lesion gives ipsilateral weakness and loss of position and vibration sense below the lesion, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature.

source_quote: If the leg is more severely affected than the arm and face (e.g., crural predominance), the lesion most likely involves the contralateral paracentral region.
vignette: A 66-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of the right leg that is much more severe than the weakness of her right arm and face. Sensation, language, and visual fields are normal.
question: Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Right paracentral region
Left lateral hemisphere, corticosubcortical
Left posterior limb of the internal capsule
Left paracentral region

explanation.why_correct: A hemiparesis in which the leg is more affected than the arm and face (crural predominance) most likely involves the paracentral region of the contralateral hemisphere, which contains the motor representation of the foot and leg. The right-sided weakness therefore points to the left hemisphere.
distractors: A right paracentral lesion would produce weakness of the left leg, not the right.
A laterally placed corticosubcortical lesion tends to cause a disproportionate faciobrachial (face and arm predominant) hemiparesis, the opposite of this pattern.
Internal capsular lesions usually cause a proportionate hemiparesis with similar weakness of face, arm, and leg; a crural-predominant pattern is only rarely seen with capsular lesions.
explanation.key_point: Crural-predominant hemiparesis suggests the contralateral paracentral region; faciobrachial predominance suggests a lateral corticosubcortical lesion.

source_quote: the lesion is generally localizable above the upper pons; likely sites are the MC, corona radiata, or internal capsule
vignette: A 71-year-old man has sudden weakness of the right arm and leg. The right side of his lower face droops, but he can wrinkle the forehead and close the eyes normally on both sides. There is no diplopia, vertigo, or other cranial nerve abnormality.
question: Where is the lesion generally localized?
options: Right lower dorsolateral pons
Right cervical spinal cord
Left motor cortex, corona radiata, or internal capsule (above the upper pons)
Right facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen

explanation.why_correct: The upper face has bilateral cortical innervation, so a supranuclear lesion spares frontalis and orbicularis oculi and weakens mainly the lower face. When this upper motor neuron type of facial paresis is on the same side as the hemiplegia, the lesion is generally above the upper pons; likely sites are the motor cortex, corona radiata, or internal capsule.
distractors: A lesion of the lower dorsolateral pons produces an ipsilateral peripheral facial paresis involving the whole half of the face, and it would be on the side opposite the limb weakness.
Spinal cord lesions do not weaken the face, so a cervical cord lesion cannot explain facial droop together with hemiparesis.
A peripheral facial nerve lesion paralyzes the upper and lower face together and does not cause arm and leg weakness.
explanation.key_point: Lower facial weakness with forehead sparing on the same side as a hemiparesis places the lesion above the upper pons.

source_quote: Anterior choroidal artery territory infarctions result in hemiparesis due to involvement of the corticospinal tract in the posterior limb of the internal capsule
vignette: A 70-year-old man has sudden weakness of the left arm and leg, reduced sensation on the entire left side of the body, and a left homonymous hemianopia. Neurologic examination shows no aphasia or neglect.
question: Which arterial territory is most likely infarcted?
options: Right recurrent artery of Heubner
Right anterior choroidal artery
Right lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery
Right anterior cerebral artery (paracentral branches)

explanation.why_correct: Anterior choroidal artery infarction damages the corticospinal tract in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (hemiparesis), the thalamic radiations in the posterior limb (hemisensory loss), and the optic tract, lateral geniculate body, or optic radiations (hemianopia). This combination of hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, and hemianopia is typical.
distractors: The recurrent artery of Heubner (from the anterior cerebral artery) supplies the anterior limb of the internal capsule, which does not explain a hemianopia or a hemisensory loss.
The lenticulostriate branches supply the superior aspect of the anterior and posterior limbs of the capsule and would not account for damage to the optic tract, geniculate body, or optic radiations.
An anterior cerebral artery infarct typically causes crural-predominant weakness without hemianopia.
explanation.key_point: Anterior choroidal artery territory infarction produces the triad of hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, and hemianopia.

source_quote: explains the facial and lingual hemiparesis with mild limb involvement observed in the capsular genu syndrome
vignette: A 66-year-old woman has sudden weakness of the left lower face and the left half of the tongue. Her left arm and leg show only mild weakness. Sensation and visual fields are normal.
question: Which part of the right internal capsule is most likely damaged?
options: Anterior limb
Posterior limb (caudal half)
Retrolenticular segment
Genu
Sublenticular segment

explanation.why_correct: Corticobulbar fibers (and perhaps motor corticopontine fibers) occupy the genu of the internal capsule. This arrangement explains the facial and lingual hemiparesis with mild limb involvement of the capsular genu syndrome.
distractors: The anterior limb contains frontopontine, thalamocortical, and corticothalamic fibers and caudate-putaminal fibers, not the main corticobulbar bundle.
The posterior limb carries the corticospinal fibers for the arm, trunk, and leg, so its lesions produce prominent limb weakness rather than predominantly face and tongue weakness.
The retrolenticular segment contains the visual radiations and corticotectal, corticonigral, and corticotegmental fibers, so a lesion there would cause visual field defects.
The sublenticular segment contains the auditory and visual radiations and would not cause facial and lingual weakness.
explanation.key_point: A capsular genu lesion causes facial and lingual weakness with mild limb involvement.

source_quote: This cortical motor hand area has been localized in the middle to lower portion of the anterior aspect of the central sulcus
vignette: A 58-year-old man has sudden isolated weakness of the left thumb and fingers, with impaired finger movements and hand flexion and extension. There is no neck or arm pain, no sensory loss, and the face, proximal arm, and leg are normal. The pattern initially suggests a cervical root problem.
question: Which cortical region is the most likely source of this isolated hand weakness?
options: Medial surface of the right precentral gyrus and anterior paracentral gyrus
Ventrolateral part of the right precentral gyrus
Middle to lower portion of the anterior aspect of the right central sulcus (Brodmann area 4)
Right postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2)
Right supplementary motor area on the medial frontal surface

explanation.why_correct: Isolated hand weakness of cortical origin, sometimes with a pseudoradicular pattern, localizes to the cortical motor hand area, in the middle to lower portion of the anterior aspect of the central sulcus (Brodmann area 4) of the hemisphere opposite the weak hand.
distractors: The medial precentral gyrus and anterior paracentral gyrus influence motor neurons of the foot, leg, and thigh, not the hand.
The ventrolateral part of the precentral gyrus contributes to the corticobulbar tract and the cranio-facial-oral musculature.
The postcentral gyrus is primary somatosensory cortex; a lesion there would mainly cause sensory loss, not isolated motor hand weakness.
The supplementary motor area lies on the medial frontal surface (Brodmann area 6) and does not represent the hand in the primary motor strip.
explanation.key_point: The cortical motor hand area lies in the middle to lower anterior wall of the central sulcus, and a lesion there can mimic a radicular hand weakness.

section: Crossed sensory loss in the medulla
source_quote: decreased pain and temperature on the ipsilateral face and contralateral body (hemianesthesia alternans)
vignette: A 57-year-old man reports numbness after a sudden episode of dizziness. Pinprick and temperature perception are decreased over the right side of his face and over his left arm, trunk, and leg. Vibration and joint position sense are normal.
question: Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Right medial medulla
Left ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
Right hemicord at the cervical level
Right lateral medulla
Left parasagittal postcentral gyrus

explanation.why_correct: A lateral medullary lesion interrupts the spinothalamic tract (contralateral loss of pain and temperature on the body) and often the spinal tract and nucleus of CN V (ipsilateral facial loss of pain and temperature), a crossed pattern called hemianesthesia alternans. The medial lemniscus can be spared.
distractors: A medial medullary lesion impairs vibration and position sense on the opposite side of the body and often causes ipsilateral CN XII paresis; pain and temperature are usually spared.
A lesion of the VPL nucleus causes loss of all sensory modalities on the opposite side of the face and body, not a crossed face and body pattern with spared position sense.
A cervical hemicord lesion produces contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion, and the face is not affected.
A lesion of the parasagittal postcentral gyrus causes sensory changes in the opposite leg, not the face and the whole opposite body.
explanation.key_point: Pain and temperature loss on the ipsilateral face and contralateral body is the sensory signature of a lateral medullary lesion.

source_quote: Impairment of vibratory and position sense on opposite side of the body, may spare the spinothalamic tract
vignette: A 63-year-old man has weakness of the right side of the tongue. Vibration and joint position sense are lost in the left arm and leg, while pinprick and temperature sensation are preserved on both sides of the body.
question: Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: Right lateral medulla
Right medial medulla
Left medial medulla
Left ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
Right dorsal column of the cervical cord

explanation.why_correct: A medial medullary lesion impairs vibratory and position sense on the opposite side of the body (medial lemniscus) and may spare the spinothalamic tract. It is often associated with ipsilateral CN XII paresis, so tongue weakness on the right with left-sided proprioceptive loss localizes to the right medial medulla.
distractors: A lateral medullary lesion mainly affects pain and temperature, which are preserved here, and would not cause tongue weakness.
A left medial medullary lesion would put the tongue weakness on the left and the proprioceptive loss on the right, the opposite of this patient.
A VPL nucleus lesion causes loss of all modalities on the opposite face and body and does not cause tongue weakness.
A dorsal column lesion in the cervical cord causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and position sense but cannot explain the tongue weakness.
explanation.key_point: Ipsilateral CN XII paresis with contralateral loss of vibration and position sense localizes to the medial medulla.

source_quote: Intrinsic cord lesions may therefore cause loss of pain, temperature, and soft touch below the level of cord damage with sparing of sacral sensation.
vignette: A 48-year-old woman has a slowly enlarging intramedullary lesion at the C5 level. Pain, temperature, and light touch are reduced in the arms, trunk, and legs below the lesion, but pinprick is normally perceived in the sacral dermatomes.
question: Which anatomic arrangement best explains the sparing of sacral sensation?
options: Sacral fibers lie most superficially in the spinothalamic tract at cervical levels
Sacral fibers lie deepest in the spinothalamic tract, next to the central gray matter
Sacral fibers ascend in the dorsal columns instead of the spinothalamic tract
Sacral fibers cross the midline in the medulla, above the level of the lesion

explanation.why_correct: The spinothalamic tract is somatotopically arranged: at cervical levels, fibers from sacral segments lie most superficially, followed by fibers from successively more rostral segments. An intrinsic lesion that compresses or destroys the deeper fibers first can therefore spare the superficial sacral fibers (sacral sparing).
distractors: If sacral fibers lay deepest, an intrinsic lesion would damage them first, producing the opposite of sacral sparing.
Pain and temperature are carried by the spinothalamic tract; the dorsal columns carry vibration, position sense, and discriminative touch.
Spinothalamic fibers decussate in the anterior commissure of the cord near their segmental level, not in the medulla.
explanation.key_point: Sacral fibers are the most superficial in the cervical spinothalamic tract, so intrinsic cord lesions spare sacral sensation.

source_quote: This disorder may be caused by bilateral dysfunction of the medial frontal cortex
vignette: A 76-year-old man has trouble starting to walk. Once moving, his feet seem glued to the floor, his turns are broken into many small steps, and he sometimes freezes. While lying down he draws figures with his feet and performs heel-to-shin movements normally. Arm swing is preserved, and there is no weakness or tremor.
question: Which pattern of dysfunction best accounts for this gait disorder?
options: Bilateral paracentral cortex
Anterior lobe of the cerebellum
Bilateral medial frontal cortex, with relative preservation of paracentral cortex
Substantia nigra
Bilateral corticospinal tracts in the cervical cord

explanation.why_correct: This is a magnetic gait: the legs can move at will and perform complex movements when tested separately, yet the feet seem glued to the floor during walking. The disorder may be caused by bilateral dysfunction of the medial frontal cortex with some preservation of the paracentral cortex.
distractors: Severe bilateral paracentral lesions produce paraplegia, not preserved voluntary leg movements.
Anterior lobe cerebellar damage (e.g., alcoholic cerebellar degeneration) causes a widened base, trunk instability, and a lurching, halting gait, not feet glued to the floor.
Parkinson disease from nigral degeneration typically shows a stooped trunk, early reduced arm swing, and short slow steps; preserved arm swing helps separate magnetic gait from it.
Bilateral corticospinal tract lesions cause a spastic gait with a narrow base and scissoring, with spasticity and hyperreflexia.
explanation.key_point: Magnetic gait reflects bilateral medial frontal dysfunction: feet glued to the floor despite normal leg movements on command.

section: Gait disorders with axial postural impairment
source_quote: A syndrome of impaired axial postural movements has been described with acute infarction or hemorrhage in the ventrolateral nucleus of the thalamus
vignette: A 71-year-old man is alert, with normal or near-normal isometric strength in the legs and mild sensory loss, after the sudden onset of symptoms. He cannot stand and could not sit up unassisted for several days. When supported, he tends to fall backward.
question: Which structure is most likely involved by the acute lesion?
options: Ventrolateral nucleus of the thalamus
Anterior lobe of the cerebellum
Ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
Subthalamic nucleus
Vestibular nuclei

explanation.why_correct: A syndrome of impaired axial postural movements (thalamic astasia), with preserved strength and inability to stand, has been described with acute infarction or hemorrhage in the ventrolateral nucleus of the thalamus or in the suprathalamic white matter. These patients fall backward or toward the side contralateral to the lesion.
distractors: Anterior lobe cerebellar damage produces a widened base, trunk instability, and lurching gait, not an inability to stand with preserved strength and falls backward.
The VPL nucleus carries somatosensory information; its lesion produces sensory loss rather than loss of axial postural control.
A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus causes hemiballismus, not an isolated failure of standing balance.
Acute vestibular lesions produce a tendency to veer or fall to the side of the lesion, rather than backward or to the contralateral side.
explanation.key_point: Acute ventrolateral thalamic lesions can cause thalamic astasia: inability to stand despite preserved strength.
